procedural_history.originating_court: Metropolitan Magistrate, Patiala House Court, Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 02.02.2016 of the High Court of Delhi in Criminal Misc. Case No. 4763 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed a petition under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code in the High Court of Delhi seeking to quash FIR No. 0139/2014 dated 20.08.2014. The High Court dismissed the petition, stating it was premature because the case was still under investigation, and directed the investigation to proceed and the Appellants to join the investigation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants filed a Special Leave Petition in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court initially granted the Appellants protection from arrest and allowed the investigation to continue. During the pendency of the appeal, the police filed a charge sheet. The Appellants then filed an amendment application seeking to also quash the charge sheet. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's judgment and order.

directions: The impugned judgment and order dated 02.02.2016 of High Court of Delhi is set aside.
The application filed by the Appellants seeking amendment of main prayer is allowed.
FIR No.0139/2014 dated 20.08.2014 and charge sheet dated 03.08.2018 are quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing an FIR is maintainable after a charge-sheet has been filed.

facts: The appellants filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) in the High Court to quash a First Information Report (FIR).
While the legal proceedings were ongoing, the police completed their investigation and filed a charge-sheet against the appellants.
The respondent argued that because a charge-sheet had been filed, the petition to quash the FIR was no longer maintainable.
law: Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. grants the High Court inherent power to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
The text of Section 482 does not contain any language that restricts the exercise of this power only to the FIR stage.
It is a settled legal principle that the High Court can exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 even when a discharge application is pending before the trial court.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that a petition to quash an FIR becomes untenable after a charge-sheet is filed.
The Court reasoned that the purpose of Section 482 is to prevent the abuse of the court's process, and this purpose is not limited to any specific stage of the proceedings.
It held that it would be a "travesty" to allow a court to interfere at the initial FIR stage but not at a later stage after the allegations have materialized into a charge-sheet.

The Court further reasoned that the abuse of process that begins with an FIR is actually "aggravated" when it progresses to a charge-sheet, making the court's intervention potentially more necessary, not less.

The Court cited its own precedent in *Joseph Salvaraj A. v. State of Gujarat*, which established that a court could still examine the merits of a case to see if offenses were prima facie made out, even after a charge-sheet had been filed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a petition filed under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash an FIR is maintainable even after a charge-sheet has been filed. The filing of a charge-sheet does not act as a bar to the High Court exercising its inherent power to prevent the abuse of the process of the court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the dispute between the parties, concerning the retention of a security deposit, constitutes a criminal offence under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: A developer (Respondent No. 2) paid a security deposit of Rs. One crore to a property owner (Appellant No. 1) as part of a development agreement.
The agreement stipulated that the deposit was to be refunded when the developer handed over the owner's share of the completed construction.
The project could not be fulfilled due to new building regulations, and the condition for the refund (handing over the constructed area) never occurred.
The developer filed an FIR alleging that the owner's retention of the security deposit constituted a criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the IPC.
The developer admitted to not having demanded the return of the money, arguing that the agreement was still in subsistence.
law: The relevant law is Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), which punishes Criminal Breach of Trust.
The court explained that the essence of this offense is the dishonest misappropriation or conversion of entrusted property in violation of a legal contract or law.
application: The Court found that the payment was a security deposit, and its retention did not amount to a dishonest conversion of entrusted property as required to constitute the offense.
The contractual obligation to refund the money had not been triggered, as the condition precedent—the developer handing over the constructed property—was never met.
The Court highlighted that the developer had not even demanded the money back, which undermined the claim of dishonest misappropriation by the owner.

The Court reasoned that there was no evidence that the owner had used or misappropriated the amount contrary to the contract. The owner had reasons to retain it, as the developer had not fulfilled other obligations.
Ultimately, the Court characterized the issue as a contractual dispute over money, which is fundamentally a civil matter, not a criminal one.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the dispute over the retention of the security deposit was civil in nature and did not constitute the criminal offense of Criminal Breach of Trust under Section 406 of the IPC.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the petition filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the FIR.

facts: The appellants had filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) to quash an FIR lodged against them.
The High Court dismissed this petition on the grounds that it was premature, as the case was still under investigation.
While the appeal was pending before the Supreme Court, the police completed their investigation and filed a charge sheet.
The respondent argued that the petition to quash the FIR was no longer maintainable because a charge sheet had since been filed.
law: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is not restricted to the FIR stage. It can be exercised even after a charge sheet has been filed to prevent the abuse of the court's process or a miscarriage of justice.

The filing of a charge sheet does not make a petition to quash the initial FIR untenable; in fact, the abuse of process caused by the FIR can be considered aggravated once it materializes into a charge sheet.
A High Court can exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. even if a discharge application is pending before the trial court.
application: The Supreme Court first addressed the procedural issue, holding that the filing of a charge sheet did not prevent the court from considering the petition to quash the proceedings. It explicitly rejected the argument that the petition had become untenable.
The Court then examined the merits of the case and found that the criminal prosecution was mala fide, untenable, and initiated solely to harass the appellants.
It determined that the dispute was essentially civil in nature and that the allegations did not constitute the offence of criminal breach of trust.
Based on these findings, the Court concluded that this was a "fit case" where the High Court should have exercised its inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in dismissing the petition. It held that the criminal proceedings were a malicious abuse of the legal process and, therefore, quashed both the FIR and the subsequent charge sheet filed against the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing an FIR is maintainable after a charge-sheet has been filed.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the petition was maintainable by filing it and appealing its dismissal, invoking the inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C.
respondent_arguments: The petition for quashing of FIR was untenable since the proceedings have gone past the stage of FIR and have resulted in a charge sheet.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the dispute between the parties, concerning the retention of a security deposit, constitutes a criminal offence under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the transactions were of a civil nature and the refund of the Rs. One crore amount was governed by a contractual clause (Clause 30 (b)), implying the dispute was a breach of contract, not a criminal offense.
respondent_arguments: The appellants committed an offence punishable under Section 406 by not returning the amount of Rs. One Crore advanced by the Respondent No.2.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the petition filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the FIR.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court was incorrect in dismissing the petition because the underlying dispute was civil in nature and did not constitute a criminal offense, and therefore the FIR should have been quashed.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the High Court was correct in its dismissal, as the petition was untenable after the filing of a charge sheet and the facts disclosed a criminal offense.

cases.principle: Cited for the principle that the High Court has the inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of the court or to secure the ends of justice.

cases.principle: Cited in the context of the High Court's power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash criminal proceedings, especially when the dispute is primarily of a civil nature.

cases.principle: Cited for the principle that the jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be exercised to prevent criminal proceedings from being used as an instrument of harassment or for settling private scores.

cases.principle: Cited for the principle that the inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly and with caution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court possesses inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, and nothing in the Code shall be deemed to limit or affect these powers.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The dispute between the parties, concerning the alleged wrongful retention of a security deposit, has the contours of a civil dispute and does not constitute a criminal offence under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code. The facts do not establish that the appellants misappropriated or dishonestly used the amount, and therefore the prosecution is mala fide, untenable, and solely intended to harass the appellants, justifying the quashing of the FIR and charge-sheet.
legal_tests_applied: A petition for quashing an FIR under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is maintainable even after a charge-sheet has been filed.

In the exercise of its inherent power under Section 482, the High Court is entitled to quash a proceeding if it concludes that allowing the proceeding to continue would be an abuse of the process of the Court or that the ends of justice require the proceeding to be quashed.

The High Court is justified in quashing a proceeding in the interest of justice when considering the veiled object behind a lame prosecution and the nature of the material on which the structure of the prosecution rests.
policy_considerations: The saving of the High Court’s inherent powers, both in civil and criminal matters, is designed to achieve a salutary public purpose which is that a court proceeding ought not to be permitted to degenerate into a weapon of harassment or persecution.
